segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Hello, Kira, how are you?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Fine thanks, Paul, how are you?

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Well, thanks. It’s good to see you. It must be twelve months since you did our course?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: That’s right. It’s nice to come back and say hello.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: What course did you enrol in?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Actually, I went straight into third-year Pharmacy. They credited me with two years, which probably made it more difficult for me.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: On the other hand, you were lucky to be granted credits. Is that why you chose the course?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Yes. And, as I’d already finished a course in it in my country [[ ]] , I thought it would be easier if I studied something I already knew.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: I didn’t realise you went into third year. I thought you started in first year. No wonder it was so hard! And what do you think is one of the big differences between studying at a university here and studying in your country?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Well, I’ve found it very difficult to write assignments, because I wasn’t familiar with that aspect of the system here. The main problem is that the lecturers expect you to be critical. That made me feel really terrible. I thought “How can I possibly do it? How can I comment on someone else’s research when they probably spent five years doing it?” I think a lot of people who come from overseas countries have similar problems. But after a while, it became easier for me. People expect you to have problems with the process of reading and writing but, in fact, it is more a question of altering your viewpoint towards academic study [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: How was the content of the lectures? Was it easy for you?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: I didn’t really have many problems understanding lectures. The content was very similar to what I’d studied before.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: And what about the lecturers themselves? Are they essentially the same as lecturers in your country?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Well actually, no. Here, they’re much easier to approach [[ ]] . After every lecture, you can go and ask them something you didn’t understand. Or you can make an appointment and talk to them about anything in the course.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Maybe you found them different because you’re a more mature student now [[ ]] , whereas when you were studying in your country you were younger and not so assertive.

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: No, I don’t think that’s the difference. Most of the students here do it. In my faculty, they all seem to make appointments – usually to talk about something in the course that’s worrying them, but sometimes just about something that might really interest them [[ ]] , something they might want to specialise in. The lecturers must set aside certain times every week when they’re available for students.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: That’s good to hear.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: And how was your timetable? Was it a very busy year?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Very, very busy. They make you work very hard. Apart from lectures, we had practical sessions in a lot of subjects. We did these in small groups [[ ]] . I had to go and work four hours every week in a community pharmacy. Actually, I enjoyed this very much – meeting new people all the time. Then in second semester, we had to get experience in hospital dispensaries, so every second day we went to one of the big hospitals and worked there [[ ]] . And on top of all that we had our assignments, which took me a lot of time. Oh, I nearly forgot, between first and second semesters, we had to work full-time for two weeks in a hospital [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: That does sound a very heavy year. So are you pleased now that you did it? Do you feel some sense of achievement?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Yeah, I do feel much more confident [[ ]] , which I suppose is the most important thing.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: And have you got any recommendations for people who are studying from overseas?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Well, I suppose they need very good English. It would be much better if they spent more time learning English before they enter the university because you can be in big trouble if you don’t understand what people are saying and you haven’t got time to translate.

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: Anything else?

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Well, as I said before, the biggest problem for me was a lack of familiarity with the education system here [[ ]] .

segments.speaker: PAUL
segments.en: It sounds as if it was a real challenge. Congratulations, Kira.

segments.speaker: KIRA
segments.en: Thanks, Paul.
